title: The Country That Votes Without Believing — Eddie Would Go

u.Nueve presidentes en diez años. Treinta: Nine presidents in ten years. Thirty-six parties on the ballot. The leading candidate at 17%. The question about Peru is no longer who will win on 12 April — it is whether the system can produce, this time, a government capable of lasting.
u.El País que Vota sin Creer: The Country That Votes Without Believing
u.Perú ha mantenido una de las economías m: Peru has sustained one of Latin America's most resilient economies through two decades of growth. At the same time it has normalised presidential instability as an ordinary mechanism for resolving political conflict. The question hanging over Lima is not who will win. It is whether the system can produce, this time, a government capable of lasting.
u.«¿En qué momento se había jodido el Perú: «At what precise moment had Peru fucked itself up?»
u.— Santiago Zavala (Zavalita), en Convers: — Santiago Zavala (Zavalita), in Conversation in the Cathedral (1969), by Mario Vargas Llosa
u.El 18 de febrero de 2026, el Congreso pe: On 18 February 2026, the Peruvian Congress elected José María Balcázar President of the Republic. He was the ninth head of state in ten years. Balcázar was 83, a member of Perú Libre — the Marxist left party that carried Pedro Castillo to power — and he had reached the presidency not through the votes of citizens but through the parliamentary arithmetic that a day earlier had removed José Jerí, his immediate predecessor, accused of unregistered meetings with Chinese businessmen. The general election was eight weeks away. The candidate leading the polls had 12% of voting intentions. Some 29% of the electorate still had no idea whom to vote for. And 64% of young people aged 18 to 29 — the Generation Z that ought to be the future of the system — said they would vote for no candidate at all.
u.Esa secuencia —remoción presidencial, su: That sequence — presidential removal, an octogenarian successor from a Marxist party, elections in eight weeks, an indifferent electorate — condenses with cruel precision the Peruvian paradox: a country that has sustained one of Latin America's most resilient economies through two decades of growth, and that has at the same time normalised presidential instability as an ordinary mechanism for resolving political conflict. The question hanging over Lima as the candidates prepare for 12 April is not who will win. It is whether the system can produce, this time, a government capable of lasting.
u.El tablero más fragmentado de la histori: The most fragmented board in history
u.Las elecciones generales del 12 de abril: The general elections of 12 April will be, according to the National Office of Electoral Processes itself, the most complex in the country's history. Not only because the ballot will list more than forty political parties, but because the first-round result — in which almost certainly no candidate will exceed 25% of valid votes — will be less a photograph of citizens' preferences than a map of their fragmentation. According to the Ipsos mock vote for Perú 21, conducted on 5 and 6 March, Rafael López Aliaga leads with 17.2% of valid votes, followed by Keiko Fujimori with 14.2%, Carlos Álvarez with 8.9% and César Acuña with 8.1%. Between them these four candidacies total less than 50%. The remaining 20% of the electorate still opts for a blank or spoilt ballot, a historically high figure.
u.La comparación con 2021 es reveladora y: The comparison with 2021 is revealing and offers no comfort. In that election, Pedro Castillo reached the run-off with 19% of the first-round vote. The system has not changed enough to prevent a candidate with minority support from reaching the ballotage. The electoral threshold, set at 5% for parties and 6% for alliances, has not contained the proliferation: in 2001 eight parties competed, in 2021 there were 18, in 2026 there are 36. The logic is perverse but coherent: in so fragmented a system, a small party can enter Congress with barely 5% of the vote, which rewards atomisation rather than coalition. The predictable result, according to analysis by the Elcano Royal Institute, is that whoever wins in April will do so on a base so narrow that the legitimacy of their exercise of power will be compromised from day one.
u.El antivoto complica aún más el panorama: The anti-vote complicates the picture further. Keiko Fujimori appears as a possible run-off candidate for the fourth consecutive time, but she also leads the anti-vote at 54%, according to the IEP. López Aliaga concentrates his support in Lima — 23.1% in the capital, 6.8% in rural Peru — which makes him a structurally weak second-round candidate against any rival with territorial roots. The most striking phenomenon of recent weeks is Wolfgang Grozo, a candidate who stood at 0.6% in February and passed 4% in the first days of March, with 12.4% among young people aged 18 to 24 — the same generation that mostly says it wants to vote for nobody.
u.El dato más revelador del estado de la d: The most revealing datum on the state of Peruvian democracy is not at the top of the polls but in the bloc that chooses no one. The 27% who in March prefer a blank ballot or no candidate — higher among the young, higher in the south, higher among those with higher education — is not indifference. It is a political verdict. Forty per cent say they will vote only to comply with the law. Sixty-five per cent say they would prefer an outsider, yet the cycle's outsiders — López Aliaga, Fujimori, Acuña — have spent decades inside the system they claim to reject.
u.Para entender por qué el electorado peru: To understand why the Peruvian electorate arrives at these elections with a mixture of exhaustion and resignation, one has to understand what has happened in the Government Palace over the past ten years. Since 2016, Peru has had Pedro Pablo Kuczynski, Martín Vizcarra, Manuel Merino, Francisco Sagasti, Pedro Castillo, Dina Boluarte, José Jerí and José María Balcázar. Eight presidents. None completed a five-year term. The principal instrument has been vacancy for 'permanent moral incapacity', a device the 1993 Constitution left deliberately ambiguous and which Congress has interpreted with a flexibility that in practice amounts to a motion of no confidence without the formal requirements of a parliamentary system.
u.La consecuencia más visible es que Perú: The most visible consequence is that Peru has a presidential system operating as a de facto parliamentary one, but without its safeguards. In a genuine parliamentary system, the leader of the party with a majority in the chamber forms a government; if it loses confidence, the government falls, not the state. In the Peruvian system, the president can be removed by a simple majority of Congress under a cause of undefined contours, but there is no 'mutual death' mechanism allowing the executive to call early elections in response. As the analyst Carlos Cabanillas noted after Jerí's removal: there is no constitutional way to resolve the crisis by calling elections. The only way out is to wait for the ones already scheduled.
u.Lo que hace este ciclo especialmente pre: What makes this cycle especially worrying is not the instability itself — Peru has been running in crisis mode for years — but the normalisation. Each new removal raises the threshold of what the system considers tolerable and lowers the political cost of the next one. The mechanisms of censure and vacancy, formally distinct, have been used in overlapping fashion within the same crisis — as happened with Jerí — exposing gaps in institutional design that no electoral reform has addressed. The incoming Congress, with 60 senators and 130 deputies elected under preferential voting among 36 parties, will be more fragmented than the current one. The architecture of instability does not disappear on 12 April.
u.El bicameralismo contra la voluntad del: Bicameralism against the will of the people
u.Una de las pocas novedades institucional: One of the few institutional novelties of these elections is also the most paradoxical. On 6 March 2024, Congress reinstated bicameralism — 60 senators in a single national district, 130 deputies under the current proportional rules — in flagrant contradiction of the 2018 referendum, in which 90% of voters had rejected precisely that reform. The technical arguments are reasonable: a Senate elected in a single district introduces a legislative brake and rebuilds the chain of accountability that the 2018 ban on re-election destroyed. But a good reform at the wrong moment can produce the opposite effect. With 36 parties and 10,000 parliamentary candidates, the new Senate could become another arena of fragmentation rather than the moderating body its defenders imagine. The first bicameral election since 1990 will take place at the worst possible moment to test that hypothesis.
u.La economía que resiste y los problemas: The economy that holds and the problems that do not
u.En ningún otro país de América Latina se: In no other Latin American country has comparable presidential instability occurred without the economic system collapsing. Nine presidents in ten years, and no financial crisis. This is no accident: an independent central bank under Julio Velarde, solid reserves, moderate debt, and copper — of which Peru is the world's second largest producer — as an external anchor in every storm. Goldman Sachs places Peru among the Latin American economies with the best growth prospects for 2026. Coface notes that mining dynamism and private consumption — 66% of GDP — have made it possible to navigate political storms that in other latitudes would have provoked severe crises. The economy, paradoxically, works well in spite of politics. But the real deficit is approaching 4.1% of GDP — twice the official figure — and whoever takes office in July will inherit that imbalance along with the accumulated pressures of electoral spending.
u.Los costos más profundos de la inestabil: The deeper costs of instability do not show up in the exchange rate or in the central bank's reserves. They show up where the state needs continuity in order to function, and Peru has gone a decade without it. The first is inequality. The Gini coefficient has held between 0.40 and 0.43 with no significant improvement despite growth: the poorest 20% receive 4% of national income, social spending per capita remains among the lowest in the region, and no government since 2016 has completed a full budget cycle with the same coalition that began it. Structural redistributive reform requires a four-year horizon. No president has had one. Labour informality — 70.9% nationally, 94.6% in the countryside — is the most visible result of that discontinuity: every government announces a formalisation plan, every presidential removal shelves it.
u.El segundo costo es la inseguridad. Los: The second cost is insecurity. Homicides rose 35.9% in 2024 — the largest proportional increase in Latin America that year — with 2,509 cases and a rate that went from 8.6 to 10.1 per 100,000 inhabitants. Lima recorded 1,012 homicides, a 28% increase on 2023. Some 81.5% of crime victims do not report the offence. None of the nine presidents was able to sustain a security policy for more than two years: plans are designed, announced and shelved with the next cabinet reshuffle. The third, and the hardest to reverse, is drug trafficking. Peru is the world's second largest producer of cocaine, with 89,755 hectares of coca in 2024 and a record 165 tonnes seized that year. The VRAEM and the coca-growing valleys are territories where the state arrives late and badly, and where organised crime — linked to Mexican, Brazilian and Albanian networks — has a permanent presence. Counter-narcotics strategy demands sustained inter-institutional coordination between the security forces, the Public Prosecutor's Office and regional governments. In Peru, that coordination restarts with every change of president. And the changes keep multiplying.
u.El presidente número diez y lo que no ca: President number ten and what does not change
u.Quien gane el 12 de abril asumirá el 28: Whoever wins on 12 April will take office on 28 July before a bicameral Congress in which no party holds a majority, with a real fiscal deficit twice the official figure, with homicides growing at twice the regional average, with drug trafficking entrenched in territories the state reaches late and badly, with 70% of the labour force in informality, and with the mechanisms of presidential removal intact — available, as always, for the next cycle. Daniel Zovatto, political scientist and regional director of International IDEA for Latin America and the Caribbean, updates Vargas Llosa's question with precision: the issue is no longer when Peru fucked itself up, but how long it can go on doing so before its economy ceases to be enough to sustain an increasingly fragile democracy. The difference between the two formulations is not rhetorical. The first looks for the origin of the collapse. The second assumes the collapse is a process already under way, and asks when it will reach the point of no return.
